title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 14–16 (Night 227, continuing nights-226), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 227 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The old man smiles at al-Asʿad, learns that he is a stranger with a brother waiting on the mountain, and offers him food from a feast without price. He leads him through a narrow lane, telling him all the way, Glory be to Him who saved you from the people of this city,, into a great house where forty aged men sit in a ring round a lit fire, worshipping it. At his call a black slave, Ghaḍbān, binds al-Asʿad and takes him down to an underground chamber, where a slave-girl beats him and feeds him a loaf and salt water morning and evening; the fire-worshippers mean to sacrifice him on the mountain at the Feast of the Fire. Waking at midnight bound and bleeding, al-Asʿad weeps for the glory he has lost — and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-seventh night,
sentences.n: The night's opening formula: the unit, al-sābiʿatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, all in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الشَّيْخَ الَّذِي لَقِيَ الْأَسْعَدَ تَبَسَّمَ فِي وَجْهِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي كَأَنَّكَ غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shaykha alladhī laqiya al-Asʿada tabassama fī wajhihi wa-qāla lahu yā waladī kaʾannaka gharībun
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-old-man who met al-Asʿad smiled in his-face and-said to-him: O my-son, as-if-you (are) a-stranger.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the old man who had met al-Asʿad smiled in his face and said to him, “My son, it seems you are a stranger here.”
sentences.n: The night opens by retelling the last words of the night before. laqiya, “to meet, come upon”, takes its object directly, without a preposition. The shadda of تبسّم is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْأَسْعَدُ نَعَمْ أَنَا غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-Asʿadu naʿam anā gharībun
sentences.l: And-said to-him al-Asʿad: Yes, I (am) a-stranger.
sentences.i: “Yes,” said al-Asʿad, “I am a stranger.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشَّيْخُ قَدْ آنَسْتَ دِيَارَنَا يَا وَلَدِي وَأَوْحَشْتَ دِيَارَ أَهْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shaykhu qad ānasta diyāranā yā waladī wa-awḥashta diyāra ahlika
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-old-man: You-have-gladdened our-dwellings, O my-son, and-you-have-made-desolate (the) dwellings (of) your-people.
sentences.i: The old man said to him, “You have brought cheer to our land, my son, and left your own people's land forlorn.
sentences.n: A courteous greeting to a newcomer built on a pair of opposites: ānasa, Form IV of ʾ-n-s, “to cheer, keep company with”, and awḥasha, Form IV of w-ḥ-sh, “to leave lonely, desolate”. diyār, plural of dār, “house”, here “homeland”. The fatḥa on the ت of آنستَ is printed; it marks the verb as “you”, not “I”.

sentences.t: فَمَا الَّذِي تُرِيدُ مِنَ السُّوقِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā alladhī turīdu mina al-sūqi
sentences.l: So-what (is) that-which you-want from the-market?
sentences.i: What is it you want from the market?”
sentences.n: mā alladhī, “what is it that”, a question built on a relative clause; the relative's pronoun (“want it”) is left unexpressed, as is usual.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَسْعَدُ يَا عَمِّ إِنَّ لِي أَخًا تَرَكْتُهُ فِى الْجَبَلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Asʿadu yā ʿammi inna lī akhan taraktuhu fī al-jabali
sentences.l: And-said al-Asʿad: O my-uncle, indeed to-me (is) a-brother, I-left-him in the-mountain.
sentences.i: Al-Asʿad said, “Uncle, I have a brother whom I left on the mountain.
sentences.n: yā ʿammi, “O uncle”, for yā ʿammī, “O my uncle”, with the -ī shortened as often in address; it is the polite way to speak to an older man, kin or not. inna lī akhan, “indeed I have a brother”: possession is “to me is”, and the possessed thing, the true subject, stands after it in the accusative of inna. taraktuhu, “I left him”, is a relative clause with no relative word, as Arabic does after an indefinite noun. The print spells fī here with ى, فى, and that is kept.

sentences.t: وَنَحْنُ مُسَافِرُونَ مِنْ بِلَادٍ بَعِيدَةٍ وَلَنَا فِى السَّفَرِ مُدَّةُ ثَلٰثَةِ شُهُورٍ
sentences.tr: wa-naḥnu musāfirūna min bilādin baʿīdatin wa-lanā fī al-safari muddatu thalāthati shuhūrin
sentences.l: And-we (are) travelling from lands far, and-to-us in the-journey (is a) period (of) three months.
sentences.i: We are travellers from a distant country, and we have been on the road three months.
sentences.n: lanā … muddatu, “to us is a period”: the same “to us is” of having, used for time spent. thalātha, “three”, takes the feminine ending with the masculine plural shuhūr, “months”, by the reverse agreement of the numbers three to ten. The dagger alif of ثلٰثة is printed: the edition's spelling, like the Qurʾān's, leaves out the long ā.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَشْرَفْنَا عَلَى هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ فَخَلَّيْتُ أَخِي الْأَكْبَرَ فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ وَجِئْتُ إِلَى هٰهُنَا لِأَشْتَرِيَ طَعَامًا وَشَيْأً وَأَعُودَ بِهِ إِلَى أَخِي مِنْ أَجْلِ أَنْ نَقْتَاتَ بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ashrafnā ʿalā hādhihi al-madīnati fa-khallaytu akhī al-akbara fawqa al-jabali wa-jiʾtu ilā hāhunā li-ashtariya ṭaʿāman wa-shayʾan wa-aʿūda bihi ilā akhī min ajli an naqtāta bihi
sentences.l: And-we-have-looked-down upon this city, so-I-left my-brother the-elder above the-mountain, and-I-came to here-here to-buy food and-a-thing and-return with-it to my-brother, for-the-sake-of that we-nourish-ourselves with-it.
sentences.i: We have come to the heights above this city, so I left my elder brother up on the mountain and came down here to buy food and a few things and take them back to him, so that we can keep ourselves alive.”
sentences.n: ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV of sh-r-f, “to look down on, overlook from a height”: ʿalā marks what lies below. khallā, Form II of kh-l-w, “to leave, let be”, is the everyday word in the later language for “leave”; its shadda, خلّيت, is printed. ilā hāhunā, “to here”, is loose but common: hāhunā is the long form of hunā with hā, “lo”. li-ashtariya, “in order to buy”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, which carries on to aʿūda. shayʾan, “something”, is spelled شيأ in the print, a habit of the edition, kept here. iqtāta bi-, Form VIII of q-w-t, “to feed on, live on”: bi- marks the food.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشَّيْخُ يَا وَلَدِي أَبْشِرْ بِكُلِّ خَيْرٍ وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّنِي عَمِلْتُ وَلِيمَةً وَعِنْدِي ضُيُوفٌ كَثِيرَةٌ وَجَمَعْتُ فِيهَا مِنْ أَطْيَبِ الطَّعَامِ وَأَحْسَنِهِ مَا تَشْتَهِيهِ النُّفُوسُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shaykhu yā waladī abshir bi-kulli khayrin wa-iʿlam annanī ʿamiltu walīmatan wa-ʿindī ḍuyūfun kathīratun wa-jamaʿtu fīhā min aṭyabi al-ṭaʿāmi wa-aḥsanihi mā tashtahīhi al-nufūsu
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-old-man: O my-son, rejoice in-every good, and-know that-I I-have-made a-feast, and-with-me (are) guests many, and-I-have-gathered in-it of (the) best (of) the-food and-its-finest what desire-it the-souls.
sentences.i: The old man said to him, “My son, take heart, all will be well. Know that I have prepared a banquet, and I have many guests, and I have laid out at it the best and finest of foods, all that the heart could desire.
sentences.n: abshir bi-, Form IV of b-sh-r, “rejoice in, take good news of”: bi- marks what is looked forward to; abshir bi-kulli khayrin is a set phrase of reassurance. walīma, “a feast, banquet”. ḍuyūfun kathīratun, “many guests”: a broken plural, even one used of persons, may take a feminine singular adjective, as here. min aṭyabi al-ṭaʿāmi … mā, “of the best of food … what”: min introduces the kind of thing that mā, “what”, stands for. tashtahīhi al-nufūsu, “the souls desire it”: nafs, “soul, self”, plural nufūs, is the seat of appetite.

sentences.t: فَهَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تَسِيرَ مَعِي إِلَى مَكَانِي فَأُعْطِيَكَ مَا تُرِيدُ وَلَا آخُذَ مِنْكَ شَيْأً وَلَا ثَمَنًا وَأُخْبِرَكَ بِأَحْوَالِ هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-hal laka an tasīra maʿī ilā makānī fa-uʿṭiyaka mā turīdu wa-lā ākhudha minka shayʾan wa-lā thamanan wa-ukhbiraka bi-aḥwāli hādhihi al-madīnati
sentences.l: So-is to-you that you-go with-me to my-place, so-that-I-give-you what you-want, and-not I-take from-you a-thing nor a-price, and-I-tell-you of-(the)-states (of) this city?
sentences.i: Will you come with me to my house? I will give you whatever you want and take nothing from you for it, no payment at all, and I will tell you how things stand in this city.
sentences.n: hal laka an, “is it yours to …?”, “would you care to …?”, a polite invitation. fa-uʿṭiyaka, “so that I may give you”: after a question, fa- of result takes the subjunctive, and ākhudha and ukhbiraka follow it. akhbara bi-, Form IV of kh-b-r, “to tell of”: bi- marks the matter told. aḥwāl, plural of ḥāl, “state, condition”, so “the state of affairs”. The madda of آخذ is printed, and shayʾan is again spelled شيأ.

sentences.t: وَالْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ يَا وَلَدِي حَيْثُ وَقَعْتُ بِكَ وَلَمْ يَقَعْ بِكَ أَحَدٌ غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: wa-al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi yā waladī ḥaythu waqaʿtu bika wa-lam yaqaʿ bika aḥadun ghayrī
sentences.l: And-the-praise (is) to-God, O my-son, where I-fell upon-you and-not fell upon-you anyone other-than-me.
sentences.i: Praise be to God, my son, that it was I who came upon you, and no one else.”
sentences.n: ḥaythu, “where”, is used in the later language for “since, in that”, giving the reason for the praise. waqaʿa bi-, “to fall in with, come upon”: bi- marks the one found. The damma on the ت of وقعتُ is printed; it marks “I”. The words are double-edged: the reader will soon learn why.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَسْعَدُ افْعَلْ مَا أَنْتَ أَهْلُهُ وَعَجِّلْ فَإِنَّ أَخِي يَنْتَظِرْلِي وَخَاطِرُهُ كُلُّهُ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Asʿadu ifʿal mā anta ahluhu wa-ʿajjil fa-inna akhī yantaẓirlī wa-khāṭiruhu kulluhu ʿindī
sentences.l: And-said al-Asʿad: Do what you (are) its-worthy-one, and-hurry, for-indeed my-brother is-waiting-for-me, and-his-mind, all-of-it, (is) with-me.
sentences.i: “Do as befits you,” said al-Asʿad, “but be quick, for my brother is waiting for me, and his every thought is with me.”
sentences.n: ifʿal mā anta ahluhu, “do that of which you are worthy”, a polite formula of acceptance: ahl, “people”, also means “one fit for, deserving of”. The shadda of عجّل is printed. ينتظرلي is doubtful: Classical Arabic would say yantaẓirunī, “he waits for me”, ينتظرني. It may be a spoken form, “waiting for me” with a colloquial li-, or a misprint for ينتظرني; it is kept as printed and read yantaẓirlī. khāṭir, “mind, thought”; khāṭiruhu ʿindī, “his mind is with me”, he is anxious about me.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ الشَّيْخُ بِيَدِ الْأَسْعَدِ وَرَجَعَ بِهِ إِلَى زُقَاقٍ ضَيِّقٍ وَصَارَ الشَّيْخُ يَتَبَسَّمُ فِي وَجْهِهِ وَيَقُولُ لَهُ سُبْحَانَ مَنْ نَجَّاكَ مِنْ أَهْلِ هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha al-shaykhu bi-yadi al-Asʿadi wa-rajaʿa bihi ilā zuqāqin ḍayyiqin wa-ṣāra al-shaykhu yatabassamu fī wajhihi wa-yaqūlu lahu subḥāna man najjāka min ahli hādhihi al-madīnati
sentences.l: And-took the-old-man by-(the)-hand (of) al-Asʿad, and-turned-back with-him to a-lane narrow, and-began the-old-man smiling in his-face and-saying to-him: Glory (to the One) who saved-you from (the) people (of) this city!
sentences.i: The old man took al-Asʿad by the hand and led him back into a narrow lane, and all the while he kept smiling in his face and saying to him, “Glory to Him who has saved you from the people of this city!”
sentences.n: akhadha bi-yadihi, “to take him by the hand”: bi- marks the part taken hold of. rajaʿa bihi, “he went back with him”, so “led him back”: bi- with a verb of motion means “taking along”. ṣāra, “to become”, with an imperfect, “began to, kept on”. subḥāna man, “glory to the One who”, an exclamation. najjā, Form II of n-j-w, “to save”; its shadda, نجّاك, is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مَاشِيًا بِهِ حَتَّى دَخَلَ دَارًا وَاسِعَةً وَفِيهَا قَاعَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal māshiyan bihi ḥattā dakhala dāran wāsiʿatan wa-fīhā qāʿatun
sentences.l: And-not he-ceased walking with-him until he-entered a-house wide, and-in-it (was) a-hall.
sentences.i: He went on walking with him until he came into a spacious house with a hall in it.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with an accusative participle, māshiyan, “walking”, means “he kept on walking”. bihi, “with him”: bi- of accompaniment, as in the sentence before. qāʿa, “a hall, a great room”.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِوَسَطِهَا أَرْبَعُونَ شَيْخًا طَاعِنُونَ فِى السِّنِّ جَالِسُونَ وَهُمْ مُجْتَمِعُونَ وَمُصْطَفُّونَ حَلْقَةً
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-wasaṭihā arbaʿūna shaykhan ṭāʿinūna fī al-sinni jālisūna wa-hum mujtamiʿūna wa-muṣṭaffūna ḥalqatan
sentences.l: And-behold, in-its-middle forty old-men, advanced in the-age, sitting, and-they (were) assembled and-ranged (in) a-ring.
sentences.i: And there in the middle of it sat forty old men, far gone in years, gathered together and ranged in a circle.
sentences.n: The print has مجتعون, a misprint for مجتمعون, corrected here. wa-idhā, “and behold”, introduces a sudden sight; here the bi- belongs to wasaṭ, “in its middle”, and simply says where. arbaʿūna shaykhan, “forty old men”: after the tens the counted noun is singular and accusative. ṭāʿinūna and jālisūna, “advanced” and “sitting”, are nominative because they agree with arbaʿūna. ṭaʿana fī al-sinni, “to be advanced in age”, literally “to thrust into the years”. iṣṭaffa, Form VIII of ṣ-f-f, “to stand in a row”; ḥalqatan, “(in) a ring”, is an accusative of the shape they make.

sentences.t: وَفِي وَسَطِهِمْ نَارٌ مُوقَدَةٌ وَالْمَشَائِخُ جَالِسُونَ حَوْلَهَا يَعْبُدُونَهَا وَيَسْجُدُونَ لَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-fī wasaṭihim nārun mūqadatun wa-al-mashāʾikhu jālisūna ḥawlahā yaʿbudūnahā wa-yasjudūna lahā
sentences.l: And-in their-middle (was) a-fire kindled, and-the-old-men sitting around-it, worshipping-it and-prostrating to-it.
sentences.i: In their midst a fire was burning, and the old men sat around it, worshipping it and bowing down before it.
sentences.n: nār, “fire”, is feminine, hence mūqadatun and the pronoun -hā. mūqad, passive participle of awqada, Form IV of w-q-d, “to kindle”. mashāʾikh, “old men, elders”, is a plural of shaykh, spelled with ئ in the print. sajada li-, “to prostrate oneself before”: li- marks the one worshipped. The old men are fire-worshippers, Magians, as the Nights pictures them.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذٰلِكَ الْأَسْعَدُ بُهِتَ لَهُمْ وَاقْشَعَرَّ بَدَنُهُ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ مَا خَبَرُهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā dhālika al-Asʿadu buhita lahum wa-iqshaʿarra badanuhu wa-lam yaʿlam mā khabaruhum
sentences.l: And-when saw that al-Asʿad, he-was-dumbstruck at-them, and-shuddered his-body, and-not he-knew what (was) their-story.
sentences.i: When al-Asʿad saw this he stood dumbfounded before them, his flesh crept, and he did not know what to make of them.
sentences.n: The object, dhālika, comes before the subject, al-Asʿadu. buhita, “to be struck dumb, dumbfounded”, is passive in form; li- marks what causes the astonishment, “at them”. iqshaʿarra, a quadriliteral Form IV of q-sh-ʿ-r, “to shiver, have one's skin creep”; its shadda, واقشعرّ, is printed, as is the hamza of رأى. khabar, “news, story”, so “what their business was”.

sentences.t: فَنَادَى الشَّيْخُ لِهٰؤُلَاءِ الْجَمَاعَةِ يَا مَشَائِخَ النَّارِ فَمَا أَبْرَكَهُ مِنْ نَهَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-nādā al-shaykhu li-hāʾulāʾi al-jamāʿati yā mashāʾikha al-nāri fa-mā abrakahu min nahārin
sentences.l: And-called the-old-man to-these the-company: O elders (of) the-fire, so-how blessed-it (is) as a-day!
sentences.i: The old man called out to the company, “O elders of the fire, what a blessed day this is!”
sentences.n: nādā li-, “to call to”: li- marks those called; Classical Arabic usually has nādā with a direct object. hāʾulāʾi, “these”, spelled in the print with ؤ. mā abrakahu, “how blessed it is!”, the verb of wonder, mā afʿalahu; min nahārin, “as a day”, says in what respect, the -hu pointing ahead to it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَادَي قَائِلًا يَا غَضْبَانُ
sentences.tr: thumma nādā qāʾilan yā Ghaḍbānu
sentences.l: Then he-called, saying: O Ghaḍbān!
sentences.i: Then he called out, “Ghaḍbān!”
sentences.n: The print spells nādā here with ي, نادي, for the ى it used a line before; it is kept, and read nādā. qāʾilan, “saying”, an accusative participle of circumstance. Ghaḍbān, “Angry”, is the slave's name.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَ لَهُ عَبْدٌ أَسْوَدُ طَوِيلُ الْقَامَةِ وَصُورَتُهُ هَائِلَةٌ بِوَجْهٍ أَعْبَسَ وَأَنْفٍ أَفْطَسَ
sentences.tr: fa-kharaja lahu ʿabdun aswadu ṭawīlu al-qāmati wa-ṣūratuhu hāʾilatun bi-wajhin aʿbasa wa-anfin afṭasa
sentences.l: And-came-out to-him a-slave black, tall (of) the-stature, and-his-form (was) fearsome, with-a-face scowling and-a-nose flat.
sentences.i: Out to him came a black slave, tall of stature and dreadful to look on, with a scowling face and a flat nose.
sentences.n: ṭawīlu al-qāmati, “long of stature”, an adjective governing a noun, the Arabic way of saying “of such-and-such a feature”. bi-wajhin, “with a face”: bi- of description. aʿbas, “frowning, scowling”, and afṭas, “flat-nosed, snub”, are on the pattern afʿal used for colours and bodily traits, and take only a fatḥa in the genitive. The ئ of هائلة is printed. Black skin, scowling face and flat nose together make up the stock portrait of the black slave that recurs throughout the Nights, where blackness and ugliness are routinely paired.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَشَارَ إِلَى الْعَبْدِ فَأَدَارَ كِتَافَ الْأَسْعَدِ فَشَدَّ وِثَاقَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma ashāra ilā al-ʿabdi fa-adāra kitāfa al-Asʿadi fa-shadda withāqahu
sentences.l: Then he-signed to the-slave, and-he-put-round (the) pinion-rope (of) al-Asʿad, and-he-tightened his-bond.
sentences.i: Then he gave the slave a sign, and the slave pinioned al-Asʿad's arms behind him and bound him fast.
sentences.n: ashāra ilā, Form IV of sh-w-r, “to make a sign to”: ilā marks the one signalled. fa-adāra kitāfa al-Asʿadi, “he passed the pinion-rope round al-Asʿad”: kitāf is the cord that ties the arms behind the back, and adāra, Form IV of d-w-r, is “to make go round”. It could also be read with the spoken kitāf, “shoulders”, “he twisted al-Asʿad's shoulders round”; either way he is pinioned. shadda withāqahu, “he tightened his bond”, tied him securely; the shadda of شدّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ قَالَ لَهُ الشَّيْخُ انْزِلْ بِهِ إِلَى الْقَاعَةِ الَّتِي تَحْتَ الْأَرْضِ وَاتْرُكْهُ هُنَاكَ وَقُلْ لِلْجَارِيَةِ الْفُلَانِيَّةِ تَتَوَلَّي عُقُوبَتَهُ بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika qāla lahu al-shaykhu inzil bihi ilā al-qāʿati allatī taḥta al-arḍi wa-utrukhu hunāka wa-qul li-al-jāriyati al-fulāniyyati tatawallā ʿuqūbatahu bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri
sentences.l: And-after that, said to-him the-old-man: Go-down with-him to the-hall which (is) under the-ground, and-leave-him there, and-say to-the-slave-girl so-and-so: she-takes-charge-of his-punishment by-the-night and-the-day.
sentences.i: After that the old man said to him, “Take him down to the hall under the ground and leave him there, and tell such-and-such a slave-girl to see to his punishment night and day.”
sentences.n: nazala bi-, “to go down with”, so “take down”: bi- of accompaniment. al-fulāniyya, “so-and-so”, the feminine of fulānī, stands in for a name the storyteller does not give. tatawallā, Form V of w-l-y, “to take charge of”, is printed with ي, تتولّي, for ى; its shadda is printed too. After qul, “say”, the order is given in the plain present, “she is to see to it”, not in the jussive. bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri, “by night and by day”: bi- of time.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهُ الْعَبْدُ وَأَنْزَلَهُ تِلْكَ الْقَاعَةَ وَسَلَّمَهُ إِلَى الْجَارِيَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahu al-ʿabdu wa-anzalahu tilka al-qāʿata wa-sallamahu ilā al-jāriyati
sentences.l: And-took-him the-slave and-brought-him-down (to) that hall, and-handed-him to the-slave-girl.
sentences.i: The slave took him and brought him down into that hall and handed him over to the slave-girl.
sentences.n: anzala, Form IV of n-z-l, “to bring down”, here takes the place reached as a direct object, tilka al-qāʿata. sallama ilā, Form II of s-l-m, “to hand over to”: ilā marks the one who receives; the shadda of سلّمه is printed.

sentences.t: فَصَارَتْ تَتَوَلَّى عُقُوبَتَهُ وَتُطْعِمُهُ رَغِيفًا وَاحِدًا بَاكِرَ النَّهَارِ وَرَغِيفًا وَاحِدًا فِى الْعِشَاءِ وَكُوزَ مَاءٍ مَالِحٍ فِى الْغَدَاةِ وَمِثْلَهُ فِى الْعَشِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣārat tatawallā ʿuqūbatahu wa-tuṭʿimuhu raghīfan wāḥidan bākira al-nahāri wa-raghīfan wāḥidan fī al-ʿishāʾi wa-kūza māʾin māliḥin fī al-ghadāti wa-mithlahu fī al-ʿashiyyi
sentences.l: And-she-began taking-charge-of his-punishment, and-feeding-him one loaf (at the) early-part (of) the-day and-one loaf at the-evening, and-a-jug (of) water salt in the-morning and-its-like in the-evening.
sentences.i: So she took his punishment in hand, and fed him a single loaf at the start of the day and a single loaf at nightfall, with a jug of salt water in the morning and another like it at evening.
sentences.n: Here tatawallā is spelled with ى and its shadda is printed. aṭʿama, Form IV of ṭ-ʿ-m, “to feed”, takes two objects, the person and the food; the jug of water is simply added to the food it gives. bākira al-nahāri, “early in the day”, an adverbial accusative of time. māʾ māliḥ, “salt water”: the later language uses māliḥ where Classical prefers milḥ. The pair al-ghadāt / al-ʿashiyy, “morning / evening”, are the old words for the two ends of the day.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَشَائِخَ قَالُوا لِبَعْضِهِمْ لَمَّا يَأْتِي أَوَانُ عِيدِ النَّارِ نَذْبَحُهُ عَلَى الْجَبَلِ وَنَتَقَرَّبُ بِهِ إِلَى النَّارِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-mashāʾikha qālū li-baʿḍihim lammā yaʾtī awānu ʿīdi al-nāri nadhbaḥuhu ʿalā al-jabali wa-nataqarrabu bihi ilā al-nāri
sentences.l: Then indeed the-elders said to-some-of-them: When comes (the) time (of the) feast (of) the-fire, we-slaughter-him on the-mountain and-we-draw-near with-him to the-fire.
sentences.i: Then the elders said to one another, “When the time of the Festival of the Fire comes round, we will sacrifice him on the mountain and offer him up to the fire.”
sentences.n: qālū li-baʿḍihim, “they said to some of them”, the later language's “to one another”: li- marks those spoken to. lammā with an imperfect, “when (it) comes”, is Middle Arabic; Classical lammā takes a past verb, and with the jussive means “not yet”. awān, “time, season”. taqarraba ilā … bi-, Form V of q-r-b, “to draw near to … by means of”, so to make an offering: bi- marks the thing offered, ilā the one it is offered to. The shadda of نتقرّب is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ نَزَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَضَرَبَتْهُ ضَرْبًا وَجِيعًا حَتَّى سَالَتِ الدِّمَاءُ مِنْ أَجْنَابِهِ وَغُمِيَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata nazalat ilayhi wa-ḍarabathu ḍarban wajīʿan ḥattā sālati al-dimāʾu min ajnābihi wa-ghumiya ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then indeed the-slave-girl came-down to-him and-beat-him a-beating painful, until flowed the-bloods from his-sides, and-it-was-swooned upon-him.
sentences.i: Then the slave-girl came down to him and beat him so cruelly that the blood ran from his sides, and he fainted away.
sentences.n: ḍarabathu ḍarban wajīʿan, “she beat him a painful beating”, the verbal noun used as an object to strengthen the verb. dimāʾ, “bloods”, plural of dam, for blood that flows. ajnāb, plural of janb, “side, flank”. ghumiya ʿalayhi, “he fainted”, literally “it was covered over him”, an impersonal passive with ʿalā marking the one who loses consciousness; the commoner form is ughmiya ʿalayhi, and the print's غمي is kept and read ghumiya.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَطَّتْ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ رَغِيفًا وَكُوزَمَاءٍ مَالِحٍ وَرَاحَتْ وَخَلَّتْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaṭṭat ʿinda raʾsihi raghīfan wa-kūza māʾin māliḥin wa-rāḥat wa-khallathu
sentences.l: Then she-set-down by his-head a-loaf and-a-jug-(of)-water salt, and-she-went and-left-him.
sentences.i: Then she set a loaf and a jug of salt water down by his head, and went away and left him.
sentences.n: The print has حظت, a misprint for حطت, corrected here. ḥaṭṭa, “to put down, set down”. The print runs كوز ماء, “a jug of water”, together as كوزماء, and that is kept. rāḥa, “to go”, is the everyday verb of going in the later language. khallathu, “she left him”, the same khallā as before; its shadda, خلّته, is printed. The hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَغْلَقَ الْأَسْعَدُ فِي نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ فَوَجَدَ رُوحَهُ مُقَيَّدًا مَضْرُوبًا وَقَدْ آلَمَهُ الضَّرْبُ
sentences.tr: fa-istaghlaqa al-Asʿadu fī niṣfi al-layli fa-wajada rūḥahu muqayyadan maḍrūban wa-qad ālamahu al-ḍarbu
sentences.l: And-al-Asʿad was-locked(?) in (the) middle (of) the-night, and-he-found his-soul fettered, beaten, and-the-beating had pained-him.
sentences.i: In the middle of the night al-Asʿad came to himself, and found himself fettered and beaten, and the beating had left him in pain.
sentences.n: فاستغلق is doubtful. istaghlaqa, Form X of gh-l-q, means “to be locked, shut fast, be obscure”, which does not fit a man waking from a swoon; the sense the story needs is “he came to”, and the likeliest repair is فاستفاق, fa-istafāqa, “he recovered his senses”, which differs from it only in the shapes of two letters, غل for فا, with the same dots. It is kept as printed and read fa-istaghlaqa, translated by the sense the story requires; whether it is a misprint or a usage unknown to the dictionaries cannot be settled here. wajada rūḥahu, “he found his soul”, the later language's “he found himself”: rūḥ, usually feminine, takes masculine adjectives here because it means the man himself. The madda of آلمه is printed.

sentences.t: فَبَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَتَذَكَّرَ مَا كَانَ فِيهِ مِنَ الْعِزِّ وَالسَّعَادَةِ وَالْمُلْكِ وَالسِّيَادَةِ وَفُرْقَةَ أَبِيهِ وَالْمُلْكَ الَّذِي كَانَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-bakā bukāʾan shadīdan wa-tadhakkara mā kāna fīhi mina al-ʿizzi wa-al-saʿādati wa-al-mulki wa-al-siyādati wa-furqata abīhi wa-al-mulka alladhī kāna fīhi
sentences.l: And-he-wept a-weeping severe, and-remembered what he-was in-it of the-might and-the-happiness, and-the-kingship and-the-lordship, and-(the)-parting (from) his-father, and-the-kingship which he-was in-it.
sentences.i: He wept bitterly, remembering the honour and happiness, the royalty and command that had once been his, and his parting from his father, and the kingdom he had lived in.
sentences.n: bakā bukāʾan shadīdan, “he wept a severe weeping”, the verbal noun again strengthening the verb. mā kāna fīhi mina …, “what he had been in, of …”: min sets out what mā covers. The sajʿ falls on al-saʿāda / al-siyāda. furqata abīhi, “the parting from his father”: the genitive marks the one parted from. The shadda of تذكّر and of العزّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
